about: Dómine, non sum dignus is not the Church's sentence but a soldier's. A centurion at Capernaum tells Jesus He need not come under his roof, and ends: sed tantum dic verbo, et sanábitur puer meus — and my servant shall be healed. The Mass keeps every word of it and changes one: ánima mea, my soul. The verse before it — Panem cæléstem — is built the same way. Cálicem salutáris accípiam, et nomen Dómini invocábo is a verse of Psalm 115, and the priest will say it unaltered in a moment over the chalice; here the cup of salvation is replaced by the bread of heaven. He says the first four words in a raised voice, striking his breast, and finishes each time under his breath — which is why the rubric stands three times.

s01.narrative: The priest genuflects, rises, and says:

s02.translation: I will take the Bread of heaven, and will call upon the name of the Lord.

s03.narrative: Bowing a little, the priest takes both halves of the Host in his left hand and slips the paten beneath them; striking his breast three times with the right, he says the following in a slightly raised voice, three times over, devoutly and humbly.

s05.narrative: The priest goes on under his breath.

s06.translation: that You should enter under my roof: but only say the word, and my soul shall be healed.

s08.narrative: The priest goes on under his breath.

s09.translation: that You should enter under my roof: but only say the word, and my soul shall be healed.

s11.narrative: The priest goes on under his breath.

s12.translation: that You should enter under my roof: but only say the word, and my soul shall be healed.

s13.narrative: The priest signs himself with the Host over the paten, and says:

s14.translation: May the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ keep my soul unto life everlasting. Amen.

s15.narrative: Bowing, the priest reverently receives both halves of the Host, lays the paten on the corporal, joins his hands and rests a while in meditation on the Most Holy Sacrament.

w002.function: An adjective, heavenly, standing where Psalm 115 has cálicem salutáris — the cup of salvation. The verse the priest says over the chalice keeps the psalm's own words; this one substitutes the bread.

w003.function: Future indicative, though the form is also the present subjunctive: “invocábo” (w007) beside it can only be future, and the two are one sentence.

w008.function: The centurion's word at Capernaum. Everything from here to “mea” (w024) is his sentence, with one word altered.

w011.function: The four words said aloud, with a blow on the breast; the rest of the sentence is finished under the breath.

w013.function: Subjunctive after ut, and the verb is intro, to walk in — an adverb intro, “inward”, exists too, but this is the verb.

w014.function: With the accusative — motion in under. The same preposition takes the ablative for resting under: sub tecto, to be under the roof.

w015.function: Tectum is what covers, from tego; the centurion means his house, and the priest means himself.

w018.function: The adverb: say the word and nothing more. It is not the neuter of tantus, which would mean so great.

w020.function: Ablative of means with “dic” (w019): speak by a word — a single utterance is enough, and no journey is needed.

w022.function: Future indicative passive: not a request but a statement of what will follow. The centurion's confidence, not his petition.

w023.function: The Gospel has puer meus, my servant; the Mass says ánima mea, and it is the only word changed.

w059.function: Subject of “custódiat” (w064): the Body keeps, and the priest says it of the Host he is holding.

w064.function: Custódio is what a guard does, not what a doctor does: the word asks for keeping safe, not for healing.

w066.function: The priest says this form over himself. The form he will say at the rail has ánimam tuam — thy soul — and nothing else in it changes.
